approaches.title: Annotation-independent test using mouse knockout phenotyping (IMPC/MGI)
approaches.method: GO and HPO overlap inherits curation bias. The International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium phenotypes knockouts systematically through a fixed pipeline, so which genes are tested for which phenotypes does not depend on prior interest. For all IMPC knockout lines that completed both morphological (skeletal, craniofacial, organ morphology) and behavioural or neurological procedures, build a 2 × 2 table: abnormal morphology yes/no versus abnormal learning-related or behavioural phenotype yes/no. Fit logistic regression of the behavioural call on the morphology call with covariates: number of other phenotype systems hit (pleiotropy), viability class and sex. Supplement with MGI curated knockouts restricted to studies reporting both kinds. Pre-registered: an adjusted odds ratio ≥ 2 (95% CI excluding 1.3) supports a shared gene set beyond pleiotropy; OR CI including 1 refutes it. Run the ion-channel and gap-junction subset separately.
steps: Pre-register phenotype term sets (MP ontology IDs), covariates and thresholds.
Download IMPC statistical results; filter to lines with both procedure classes; record version and checksums.
Fit adjusted logistic models for all genes and the bioelectric subset.
Compare with approach 1 to see whether annotation-based and screen-based answers agree.
approaches.decisive_result: An adjusted odds ratio, with CI, for co-occurrence of morphological and behavioural or learning phenotypes in systematically phenotyped knockouts. This is the strongest available test free of curation bias.
approaches.failure_signature: IMPC behavioural procedures measure activity and anxiety rather than learning per se, so the 'learning' category cannot be operationalized; the test then reverts to a broader behavioural proxy, which must be stated as a reinterpretation.

approaches.title: Mechanistic proximity: network separation of the two modules in INDRA's causal graph
approaches.method: Overlap counts shared members. TAME's claim is better read as shared machinery: the modules may be mechanistically adjacent without sharing genes. Use the network separation s_AB = ⟨d_AB⟩ − (⟨d_AA⟩ + ⟨d_BB⟩)/2 of Menche et al. 2015, computed on INDRA CoGEx's causal statement graph between human genes (indra_rel edges with evidence_count ≥ 2, undirected for distance). A = core morphogenesis set and B = core learning/memory set (experimental GO annotations), with SynGO synaptic genes as a positive-control module expected to be near B. Null: degree-preserving randomization, sampling gene sets with matched degree distribution (binned), 10^4 draws. Pre-registered: s_AB < 0 with z < −3 against the degree-matched null supports shared machinery; s_AB ≥ 0 refutes it. Repeat after removing the top 1% highest-degree hubs to check that shared housekeeping hubs do not drive proximity.
steps: Pre-register edge filters, gene sets, null and thresholds.
Export the INDRA causal subgraph via execute_cypher; record the query and statement-hash counts.
Compute s_AB and the null distribution; run the hub-removal sensitivity check.
For gene pairs driving proximity, cite INDRA statement hashes and PMIDs as mechanistic evidence.
approaches.decisive_result: Network separation s_AB with z-score against a degree-matched null, with and without hubs. Negative separation surviving hub removal would support Levin's shared-machinery prediction in a form the overlap test cannot detect; non-negative separation would refute it.
approaches.failure_signature: INDRA's causal graph is so dominated by literature-heavy genes that degree matching cannot remove study bias (separation tracks publication count), so the result reflects literature structure rather than biology.

approaches.title: Degree-matched ontology overlap test
approaches.method: Freeze GO terms for morphogenesis and learning or memory, propagate annotations under a declared relation set, and restrict to experimentally supported human and mouse genes. Test overlap against 100000 permutations matched jointly on total annotation count, publication count, protein-interaction degree and gene length; repeat after removing generic signaling and housekeeping terms.
steps: Timestamp ontology and evidence-code filters before retrieving genes.
Fit propensity scores for membership in each gene set from bias covariates.
Compute matched-null overlap z score, odds ratio and semantic-specificity-weighted overlap.
Repeat for ion-channel and gap-junction genes and across species.
approaches.decisive_result: Wide overlap requires odds ratio at least 2, empirical P below 0.001 and replication in both human and mouse after generic-term removal; an odds ratio between 0.8 and 1.25 supports no enrichment.
approaches.failure_signature: Balance diagnostics retain standardized covariate differences above 0.1 or enrichment disappears under leave-one-ontology-term-out analysis.

approaches.title: Mechanistic-pathway convergence in INDRA
approaches.method: Move beyond gene lists by constructing evidence-weighted INDRA subnetworks connecting curated morphogenesis phenotypes and learning phenotypes. Compare shared causal intermediates and signed paths to degree-preserving, evidence-count-matched network rewires; require statement-level provenance and hold out papers mentioning both domains.
steps: Ground phenotype-associated genes and retain statements with primary evidence.
Remove cross-domain papers to prevent literature leakage.
Compute shared intermediates, signed-path enrichment and pathway conductance.
Run 10000 constrained rewires preserving node degree and statement evidence bins.
approaches.decisive_result: Mechanistic convergence requires at least twofold excess shared intermediates with empirical P below 0.001 and replication after removing all ion-channel genes; null-level paths refute broad convergence.
approaches.failure_signature: The result is driven by fewer than five hubs or by statements from cross-domain review papers.
approaches.missing: INDRA literature coverage and causal direction are uneven across developmental systems.

approaches.title: Pleiotropy-matched overlap of morphogenesis and learning genes
approaches.method: Pre-register human genes with GO:0009653 (anatomical structure morphogenesis) and GO:0007611 (learning or memory). Primary run excludes evidence code IEA; a second run includes it and is labeled. Background is human protein-coding genes. The statistic is the odds ratio of the intersection. The null is 10,000 permutations that preserve both set sizes and match genes on the number of GO annotations and on degree in the public INDRA statement graph. Wide overlap, the pre-registered threshold, is an odds ratio above 2 and a permutation p-value below 0.01. The same threshold is a primary endpoint, not a subgroup glance, for the subsets annotated with GO:0005216 (monoatomic ion channel activity; the synonym is ion channel activity) and with GO:0005921 (gap junction). Housekeeping is partly absorbed by the annotation-count match; it is not a separate covariate invented after the test.
steps: Freeze the two GO sets, the IEA rule, the odds-ratio threshold and the permutation scheme.
Pull annotations from Gene Ontology and degrees from INDRA.
Compute the observed odds ratio.
Run 10,000 matched permutations.
Apply the same test to the ion-channel and gap-junction subsets as primary endpoints.
approaches.decisive_result: Odds ratio above 2 and permutation p below 0.01 for the full sets and, separately, for the ion-channel subset and the gap-junction subset.
approaches.failure_signature: The full-set odds ratio falls inside the matched null. That refutes wide overlap beyond pleiotropy and annotation volume. A hit that appears only in the IEA-included run is annotation noise and does not count.

approaches.title: INDRA statement density inside the intersection
approaches.method: Set overlap can be shared annotation fashion. This test asks whether genes in the intersection are mechanistically tied. Count INDRA statements with evidence count at least 5 that connect a GO:0009653 gene to a GO:0007611 gene. Compare with 10,000 random bipartitions that preserve the two set sizes and the joint degree sequence. The pre-registered effect is a statement count above the 99th percentile of that null. Repeat for the ion-channel subset and the gap-junction subset. A gene-set hit with a null statement density means the shared genes are not preferentially wired to each other in INDRA, which is a different negative from a failed overlap test.
steps: Build the morphogenesis and learning sets as in the overlap test.
Count INDRA statements of evidence count at least 5 across the cut.
Permute bipartitions preserving sizes and degrees, 10,000 times.
Apply the 99th-percentile threshold.
Repeat for ion channels and gap junctions.
approaches.decisive_result: Cross-set INDRA statement count above the 99th percentile of the degree-preserving null, overall and in the two bioelectric subsets.
approaches.failure_signature: The count lies within the null. Overlap of annotations, if it exists, is then not matched by INDRA evidence between the sets.

approaches.title: Repeat the overlap using only pre-2015 annotations
approaches.method: Annotation fashion after Levin's papers would inflate overlap. Repeat the matched odds-ratio test using only GO annotations whose assignment date is before 2015, if QuickGO exposes that date. Keep the same sets, the same exclusion of IEA, and the same thresholds. If dates are not in the download, the approach stops as inconclusive rather than using a proxy such as the paper's publication year. A signal present in the full ontology and absent before 2015 is evidence of later annotation, not of a standing shared gene set. A signal present before 2015 survives that objection.
steps: Check whether annotation dates are present before computing the odds ratio.
Restrict to dates before 2015.
Reuse the matched permutation null.
Apply the odds-ratio and p-value thresholds.
If dates are absent, record inconclusive and stop.
approaches.decisive_result: The pre-2015 odds ratio either clears the same threshold as the full test or it does not. Clearing it supports overlap that predates the recent annotation wave.
approaches.failure_signature: The pre-2015 odds ratio falls inside the null while the full-ontology test does not. The apparent overlap is then carried by later annotations.
approaches.missing: GO assignment dates may be absent from the query used. The approach then cannot run, and that is a stated stop.

problems.title: Does the bioelectric prepattern predict anatomical outcome?
problems.question: Is there a quantitative, predictive mapping from a measured resting-potential (Vmem) pattern in a tissue to the anatomical structure it will form, such that perturbing the pattern predicts the anatomical change before it occurs?
problems.known_state: Levin and colleagues report that Vmem patterns prefigure and can instruct anatomy in planarian head regeneration, Xenopus face and eye induction, and tumour induction (Levin and Martyniuk 2018). BETSE (Pietak and Levin 2016) simulates Vmem dynamics; Durant et al. (2017) modelled planarian anterior-posterior polarity. No model takes an arbitrary measured Vmem map and outputs a falsifiable anatomical prediction with stated accuracy. Thirteen Levin tests in the repo are pre-registered and awaiting data.
acceptance_criteria: A model (bounded bioelectric simulation plus a pattern-to-anatomy decoder) that, given published Vmem images of perturbed and control embryos or planarian fragments, predicts the anatomical phenotype class with pre-registered accuracy on held-out images.
Explicit statement of which published datasets are used for training and which for testing.
falsifiers: Prediction accuracy at chance on held-out perturbations refutes the predictive form of the bioelectric-code hypothesis for those tissues.
problems.data_access: Published Vmem imaging (DiBAC/CC2-DMPE) in open-access Levin lab papers; BETSE (open source).

related_claims.label: Hexanol, which does not block gap junctions, does not alter head shape
HCN2 modelled as a voltage-controlled switch that amplifies small Vmem gradients
Native HCN2 activity is not required for normal brain patterning
Animal senses use the same ion channel mechanisms found in bacteria

approaches.title: Curated Vmem image corpus and a decoder validated by leave-one-study-out
approaches.method: Build an image corpus from open-access Levin-lab and other papers showing voltage-reporter dye images (DiBAC4(3), CC2-DMPE:DiSBAC2(3)) of control and perturbed Xenopus embryos and planarian fragments, each linked to the reported anatomical outcome class: for Xenopus craniofacial or eye, normal, ectopic eye, malformed face; for planaria, one head, two heads, no head. Register images to a common template (embryo outline or fragment axis), extract a low-dimensional Vmem feature vector (template-aligned intensity on a coarse grid, normalized to within-image range because dye images are not absolutely calibrated). Train simple, pre-registered decoders (multinomial logistic regression on 20 PCA components; k-NN) and evaluate leave-one-study-out, so test images come from papers not used in training. Pre-registered success: balanced accuracy ≥ 0.70 against a chance level computed from class frequencies, permutation p < 0.01.
steps: Pre-register inclusion criteria (open licence, dye named, outcome reported for the imaged individual or the imaged group), decoder, features and threshold.
Harvest figures with their licences; annotate outcome labels from the papers' text; record provenance.
Register images and extract features via the morpholib pipeline where applicable.
Run leave-one-study-out evaluation and the permutation test; report confusion matrices.
approaches.decisive_result: Leave-one-study-out balanced accuracy of anatomy-class prediction from Vmem images, against chance, with a permutation p-value. Above 0.70 supports a predictive mapping; at chance refutes the predictive form for those tissues.
approaches.failure_signature: Most published Vmem images show group-representative embryos without individual outcome labels, or too few studies (fewer than 5 per tissue) exist for leave-one-study-out: inconclusive, data-unavailable.
approaches.missing: Raw image data with individual-level outcome labels are rarely published; the swarm cannot generate new imaging.

approaches.title: Pre-registered forward predictions of perturbation outcomes from bioelectric simulation
approaches.method: Test the instructive (causal) form of the hypothesis on perturbations whose outcomes are published but held out from calibration. Calibrate a BETSE or frontier_simulate model of the planarian fragment (ion channels, pumps, gap junctions per Durant et al. 2017 and Pietak and Levin 2017) on control and two perturbation conditions only. Then, for each held-out perturbation in the literature (for example ivermectin-induced hyperpolarization, SCH-28080 H,K-ATPase inhibition, octanol gap-junction block at stated concentrations), predict the steady-state anterior–posterior Vmem pattern. Map it to anatomy with a rule fixed in advance: a depolarized region above threshold θ predicts a head, θ fixed from the calibration conditions. Lodge predictions as a timestamped commit before comparison. Score the fraction of held-out perturbations whose predicted outcome class matches the published one, against a baseline that always predicts the most common outcome.
steps: Fix model structure and calibration conditions; pre-register the Vmem-to-anatomy rule and the held-out list.
Calibrate parameters on the calibration set; freeze.
Simulate each held-out perturbation; commit predictions before reading outcomes.
Compare with published outcomes; report accuracy against the baseline with a binomial test.
approaches.decisive_result: The fraction of held-out pharmacological and genetic perturbations whose anatomical outcome class the frozen model predicts, against the most-common-class baseline. Accuracy significantly above baseline (binomial p < 0.01, at least 10 held-out conditions) supports the predictive bioelectric code; baseline accuracy refutes this model's version of it.
approaches.failure_signature: Too few held-out perturbations with clear published outcomes and known molecular targets (fewer than 10), or model outcomes so sensitive to unmeasured parameters that predictions are not robust to plausible parameter ranges (report the fraction of the parameter posterior agreeing).
approaches.missing: frontier_simulate offers bounded previews only; full BETSE calibration needs more compute and parameter data (channel densities) than published papers supply.

approaches.title: Dose–response meta-analysis: does Vmem shift size predict penetrance?
approaches.method: A predictive code implies graded dependence: larger, more localized Vmem shifts should give higher penetrance of the predicted phenotype. Code every published bioelectric perturbation experiment in Xenopus and planaria reporting both (a) a quantitative Vmem change (reporter intensity ratio or electrode mV, with dispersion) and (b) phenotype penetrance (k of n animals). Fit a random-effects logistic meta-regression of penetrance on the standardized Vmem shift, with study as a random effect and tissue and perturbation class (channel misexpression, drug, gap-junction block) as covariates. Pre-registered: a positive slope with 95% CI excluding 0, and the shift explaining ≥ 30% of between-condition variance, support the graded predictive form; a slope CI including 0 refutes it. Check small-study effects with funnel plots and Egger's test, since positive results may be preferentially published.
steps: Pre-register extraction rules, effect-size standardization and the model.
Systematically search open-access literature; double-extract data (two independent agents) and reconcile.
Fit the meta-regression; run publication-bias diagnostics.
Link each coded study to repo claims (levin-2018-hcn2, levin-2019-boundary) and record evidence.
approaches.decisive_result: The meta-regression slope of phenotype penetrance on Vmem shift magnitude with CI, and the variance explained, adjusted for publication bias.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 15 conditions report both a quantitative Vmem change and penetrance, or Egger's test shows strong small-study bias making the slope uninterpretable.

approaches.title: Held-perturbation Vmem phenotype decoder
approaches.method: Digitize raw or supplementary Vmem images with specimen-level anatomical outcomes from one system only. Register maps to a common coordinate frame, train a spatial decoder on controls and selected perturbation classes, and hold out entire intervention mechanisms so the test measures pattern-based transfer rather than batch recognition.
steps: Require at least 200 specimens, five perturbations and 30 specimens per held-out class.
Freeze normalization, masks and phenotype labels before model training.
Compare Vmem decoder with morphology-at-imaging-time, batch and permuted-map baselines.
Use nested cross-validation grouped by experiment and intervention.
approaches.decisive_result: Predictive mapping requires held-intervention macro-F1 at least 0.75 and at least 0.15 above every baseline, with bootstrap 95% lower bound above 0.6.
approaches.failure_signature: Performance falls to chance when experiments or intervention mechanisms are held out, indicating batch-specific correlation rather than a transferable code.
approaches.missing: Specimen-linked raw Vmem maps and later phenotype labels may not be publicly available at adequate sample size.

approaches.title: Intervention-generalizing bioelectric simulator
approaches.method: Construct a bounded tissue graph with measured channel classes, gap-junction coupling and cell-state transitions. Fit conductances only on control and one perturbation, then predict spatial Vmem and phenotype under unseen channel, gap-junction and pump interventions. Compare mechanistic predictions to a flexible image-only decoder.
steps: Ground intervention targets and signed channel effects through INDRA CoGEx.
Specify prior parameter ranges and identifiability checks.
Calibrate with simulation-based inference on preregistered training interventions.
Predict held-out Vmem maps and anatomical classes without parameter refitting.
approaches.decisive_result: Mechanistic support requires held-intervention Vmem spatial correlation above 0.7 and phenotype accuracy above 0.75 for at least three distinct intervention classes.
approaches.failure_signature: No single posterior parameter region predicts both Vmem and anatomy, or image-only prediction strongly outperforms simulation on held interventions.
approaches.missing: Quantitative conductance, coupling and longitudinal imaging data for the same specimens.

approaches.title: Leave-one-paper-out decoder of published Vmem figures
approaches.method: Admissible images are the voltage-reporter figures (DiBAC or CC2-DMPE) in the open-access papers of Levin and Martyniuk 2018, Pietak and Levin 2016, and Durant et al. 2017, with the phenotype class taken from the caption: for planaria, two-headed, normal, or no-head; for the other tissues, the classes the caption itself names. Features, frozen first, are the anterior-posterior dipole of the reported potential, the number of domains above the caption's own threshold, and a left-right asymmetry index. The split is by paper: train on two, test on the third, all three rotations. Support requires accuracy at least 0.7 and a binomial test against the test paper's majority class at p below 0.05, in at least two rotations. Independent experiments, not panels of one experiment, are the sample. Fewer than 20 independent experiments across the three papers makes the test underpowered. Raw stacks are not required and are not invented.
steps: Freeze features, classes and the 0.7 accuracy bar before measuring figures.
Encode each admissible figure's features from the published image and its caption.
Rotate training and test by paper.
Score accuracy against the majority-class baseline.
Stop as underpowered if fewer than 20 independent experiments exist.
approaches.decisive_result: Accuracy at least 0.7 and above the majority class at p below 0.05 in at least two of three paper rotations, on at least 20 independent experiments.
approaches.failure_signature: Accuracy consistent with the majority class in two or more rotations. The dipole-and-domain decoder then does not predict anatomy on these figures.
approaches.missing: Raw microscopy. Published figures are a biased subset of the experiments, and the test cannot repair that.

approaches.title: Freeze BETSE parameters and predict a held-out perturbation
approaches.method: Use the BETSE engine. Fix parameters at the published defaults in Pietak and Levin 2016 before looking at outcome counts. Choose one channel-block or gap-junction perturbation that Durant et al. 2017 report and that was not used to set those defaults. Map the simulated anterior-posterior Vmem difference onto the phenotype classes with a threshold frozen from the control simulation alone. Compare the predicted class with the published outcome. frontier_simulate may be called only as a bounded bioelectric preview to see whether a parameter dictionary is inside its allowlisted family. Its ephemeral result is not evidence and cannot meet this test. Success is the correct class on that held-out perturbation and on one additional perturbation from the same paper, both chosen before the run.
steps: Pin the BETSE commit and the published default parameters.
Name the two held-out perturbations before simulating.
Derive the decision threshold from the control simulation only.
Simulate the two perturbations and emit phenotype classes.
Score them against the paper. Do not retune.
approaches.decisive_result: Both pre-named held-out perturbations assigned the published phenotype class by the frozen threshold.
approaches.failure_signature: Either perturbation is misclassified. Retuning parameters to obtain the class fails the approach.
approaches.missing: frontier_simulate is a bounded preview and is not a substitute for BETSE. The swarm still needs a local BETSE run for the evidence.

approaches.title: Prove which Vmem summaries cannot identify anatomy
approaches.method: A decoder that sees only the anterior-posterior dipole and the number of supra-threshold domains assigns the same phenotype to any two fields that agree on those summaries. Prove that statement. Then apply it to the admissible figures: search for two experiments with different caption phenotypes whose dipole and domain count agree within a tolerance frozen first (relative dipole difference below 0.1, same domain count). A hit refutes every decoder that uses only those features. Absence of a hit does not confirm the bioelectric code; it only says these features are not yet contradicted by the figures. This approach can refute a feature set that the classifier approach would merely score as inaccurate.
steps: Prove the identifiability lemma for dipole and domain count.
Freeze the 0.1 relative tolerance.
Measure the summaries on the admissible figures.
Search for a cross-phenotype collision under that tolerance.
Report a refuting pair or the absence of one.
approaches.decisive_result: Either a pair of published experiments with different phenotypes and summaries inside the tolerance, which refutes dipole-and-domain decoders, or an exhaustive statement that no such pair exists in the admissible figures.
approaches.failure_signature: The lemma is false for some pair of fields, which would be a mathematics error, or the figure measurements are too coarse to decide equality within 0.1, in which case the empirical half is inconclusive.
approaches.missing: Raw pixel values. Figure measurements may be too coarse for the 0.1 tolerance, and the approach then stops as inconclusive on the empirical half.

problems.title: Is memory in gene regulatory network models generic or a biological signature?
problems.question: Do the memory and habituation behaviours found in published ODE models of biological pathways occur at the same rate in random nonlinear ODE networks of matched size, sparsity and kinetics, or are they enriched in biological networks?
problems.known_state: Biswas, Manicka, Hoel and Levin (2021) found several kinds of memory (UCS-based, pairing, associative, consolidation) in 35 BioModels pathway models, and habituation in 27 of them (levin-2022-grn-learning claims, top of the repo's testability ranking). No matched random-network null has been run, so it is unknown whether the result says anything about biology rather than about nonlinear dynamics in general.
acceptance_criteria: A pre-registered computational test re-running the Biswas protocol on the original 35 models and on at least 350 random networks matched on node count, edge density, kinetic form and parameter ranges; the enrichment statistic and its threshold stated in advance.
Code and seeds published so the result is reproducible.
falsifiers: Memory rates in random networks equal to or above the biological ones refute the biological-signature reading.
problems.data_access: BioModels (open), Biswas et al. 2021 code (open access paper).

related_claims.label: Published ODE models of gene and protein pathways show several kinds of memory
Pathway memories can form through dynamics alone, without structural change
Most pathway-model memories persist over long periods and survive recall
Habituation (pharmacoresistance) occurs in every testable pathway model
Stimulating other nodes can break pharmacoresistance in many pathway models

approaches.title: Re-run the Biswas protocol on 35 BioModels and ≥ 350 matched random ODE networks
approaches.method: Reimplement the Biswas et al. 2021 protocol: choose stimulus nodes (UCS, CS) and a response node, apply the stimulus schedules for each memory type (UCS-based, pairing, transfer, associative, consolidation) and score memory by the paper's criteria and thresholds. Validate by reproducing their per-model memory calls on the 35 BioModels models (agreement ≥ 90% required before proceeding). Null ensemble: for each biological model, generate 10 random networks matched on node count, edge count and density, in- and out-degree sequences (configuration model), kinetic forms (mass-action and Hill terms in the same proportions, with Hill coefficients drawn from the model's empirical distribution), parameter values drawn from the model's own log-parameter distribution, and stability (retain only networks with a stable steady state from the default initial condition, as biological models have). Simulate with libRoadRunner. Statistic: per memory type, the fraction of (network, stimulus/response triple) combinations showing memory, biological versus random. Pre-registered: 'biological signature' if the biological rate exceeds the random rate by ≥ 2× with a stratified permutation p < 0.01; 'generic' if the ratio is ≤ 1.2.
steps: Reimplement the protocol; validate against the paper's reported calls; publish the discrepancy list.
Write result.json with matching criteria, statistic and thresholds before simulating random networks.
Generate ≥ 350 matched random networks; check matching statistics.
Run all protocols; compute rates and ratios with stratified permutation p-values; publish code and seeds.
approaches.decisive_result: Per memory type, the ratio of memory rates in biological versus matched random networks with permutation p. A ratio ≥ 2 supports the biological-signature reading and ≤ 1.2 supports 'generic nonlinear dynamics', which is the problem's stated falsifier.
approaches.failure_signature: Reproduction of the original calls falls below 90% agreement because protocol details are underspecified in the paper, so any comparison tests a different protocol.

approaches.title: Attribution by surgery: rewire topology vs shuffle parameters in real models
approaches.method: Random networks differ from biological ones in many ways at once. A sharper design perturbs the biological models themselves along one axis at a time. For each of the 35 models: (a) topology surgery, degree-preserving edge swaps (100 swaps per edge) keeping every reaction's rate law and parameters; (b) parameter surgery, permuting parameter values among reactions of the same kinetic type, keeping topology; (c) kinetic surgery, replacing Hill terms with Michaelis–Menten terms (n = 1), keeping topology and parameters; (d) a combination. Generate 20 variants per model per surgery, discard variants without a stable steady state, and re-run the memory protocol. Memory that survives (a) but not (b) points to tuned parameters; memory surviving (b) but lost under (c) points to cooperativity (ultrasensitivity) as the generic cause. This decomposes any biological enrichment from approach 1 into causes.
steps: Implement SBML-level surgery operators with libsbml; verify that variants remain valid and stable.
Pre-register the attribution logic (which surgery outcomes imply which cause).
Run the memory protocol on all variants.
Report per-memory-type retention rates under each surgery with CIs.
approaches.decisive_result: Retention rates of each memory type under topology, parameter and kinetic surgery. For example, '80% of UCS memory survives topology rewiring but only 20% survives replacing Hill terms' would identify ultrasensitivity, not network wiring, as the cause.
approaches.failure_signature: Most surgical variants lose steady-state stability, so the surviving variants are a biased subset and retention rates are uninterpretable.

approaches.title: Theory: memory as multistability or slow manifolds, predicted by CRNT
approaches.method: Explain which networks can show which memory, so the result is a theorem plus a prediction rather than only a rate comparison. Step 1 (proof): show that, for the protocol's definitions, persistent UCS-based memory over a test window T after stimulus removal requires either (i) multistability, with the stimulus switching basins, or (ii) a slow variable with relaxation time ≥ T. The argument: if the system is monostable with all eigenvalues at the steady state having real part ≤ −λ and the steady state is globally attracting with exponential rate λ, the response returns within ε after time log(C/ε)/λ, so memory beyond that is impossible. Formalize the linear-stability core in Lean. Step 2 (prediction): for mass-action models, Chemical Reaction Network Theory (deficiency zero and deficiency one theorems) certifies that some networks cannot be multistable for any rates. Classify all 35 models and the random ensemble by CRNT before simulation; predict that CRNT-certified monostable networks show long-window memory only if they have slow eigenvalues (computed). Compare with approach 1's observed memory calls.
steps: State and prove the exponential-relaxation lemma for monostable systems in Lean (linear case; nonlinear case by citation of standard Lyapunov results with stated hypotheses).
Run CRNT analysis (deficiency computation) on mass-action-convertible models; compute slowest eigenvalues at steady state.
Pre-register predicted memory or no-memory per model from (multistability possible, slowest timescale).
Compare predictions with observed memory calls; report sensitivity and specificity.
approaches.decisive_result: A proved necessary condition for persistent memory, and the accuracy with which the CRNT plus slowest-timescale classification predicts observed memory across biological and random networks. High accuracy (≥ 85%) shows memory is explained by generic dynamical features, whatever the biological enrichment.
approaches.failure_signature: Many networks show memory the classification rules out, which would mean the protocol's memory criterion picks up transient effects within the test window, a finding about the protocol itself; or most models use non-mass-action kinetics outside CRNT's scope.
approaches.missing: Many BioModels use non-mass-action rate laws; CRNT results cover only a subset.

approaches.title: Matched random-network memory enrichment test
approaches.method: Reimplement the exact stimulation and memory criteria for all 35 biological ODE models, then generate 100 matched nulls per model preserving node count, signed degree sequence, kinetic-law family, parameter marginal distributions and stiffness. Blindly apply identical protocols and estimate enrichment with a model-paired conditional logistic regression.
steps: Freeze executable model versions and numerical tolerances.
Validate protocol reproduction against all reported memory calls.
Generate at least 3500 convergent null networks with fixed seeds.
Classify memory, habituation and consolidation using preregistered effect thresholds.
approaches.decisive_result: Biological enrichment requires paired odds ratio at least 2 with 99% interval excluding 1 for a memory class and replication across two null generators; odds ratio at or below 1 refutes enrichment.
approaches.failure_signature: Fewer than 80% of published calls reproduce or null convergence filtering changes network dynamics enough to break covariate balance.

approaches.title: Dynamical motif attribution of memory
approaches.method: Identify whether memory enrichment is explained by specific feedback motifs rather than biological origin. Enumerate signed three- and four-node motifs, sample kinetic parameters by Latin hypercube, and estimate each motif's memory probability. Decompose each BioModels network's prediction with motif counts and targeted edge ablations.
steps: Enumerate nonisomorphic signed motifs with self-loops handled explicitly.
Run at least 10000 parameter sets per motif under the fixed memory protocol.
Fit a sparse hierarchical predictor from motif content to memory behavior.
Ablate predicted motifs in biological models and matched nulls.
approaches.decisive_result: A motif mechanism is established if its presence increases memory probability by at least 0.25 and deleting it abolishes memory in at least 80% of predicted biological models while matched control deletions do not.
approaches.failure_signature: Memory depends on diffuse parameter combinations and no motif has stable effects across kinetic families.
approaches.missing: Combinatorial parameter sweeps are expensive and motif effects may be context-dependent.

approaches.title: Match 350 random ODE networks to the 35 BioModels
approaches.method: Re-run the Biswas, Manicka, Hoel and Levin 2021 memory probes on the original models they took from BioModels, and on at least 10 random networks per model, at least 350 in total. Match each random network on node count, reaction count, and kinetic family (mass-action or Hill, matching the source model). Draw parameter magnitudes from the empirical distribution of the absolute values in that source model. Randomize regulatory signs in this approach; the topology-preserving arm is the next one. Probes are the paper's UCS-based, pairing, associative and consolidation memories, plus habituation. The enrichment statistic is the paired difference in the number of memory kinds present. Success, pre-registered, is a permutation p-value below 0.01 against the random ensemble and at least 20 of the 35 biological models showing strictly more memory kinds than their matched random networks. Publish seeds and the model identifiers.
steps: Pin the 35 BioModels identifiers from the paper before simulating.
Build at least 10 matched random networks for each, signs randomized.
Run the five probes with the paper's protocol.
Compute the paired permutation test.
Require p below 0.01 and at least 20 of 35 models strictly enriched.
approaches.decisive_result: Permutation p below 0.01 and strict enrichment in at least 20 of 35 models. Otherwise memory in this protocol is not enriched relative to the matched random networks.
approaches.failure_signature: The random networks meet or exceed the biological memory rate. That refutes the biological-signature reading for this match. A probe implementation that cannot reproduce the paper's count on the original 35 models invalidates the run before the null is interpreted.

approaches.title: Factor topology against kinetics in the memory rate
approaches.method: Cross two factors the single matched null confounds. Arm A keeps the biological reaction graph and redraws parameters from the same magnitude distribution. Arm B rewires the graph to the same degree sequence and keeps the original parameters. Arm C does both and is the null from the first approach. Each arm has the same 10 networks per model. The biological-signature claim for topology survives only if arm A still shows the enrichment and arm B does not. The claim for kinetics survives only if arm B shows it and arm A does not. If arm A already loses the enrichment, topology is not the carrier. Pre-register that split before looking at which arm wins.
steps: Build arms A, B and C with the shared size match.
Run the same five probes.
Test enrichment separately in each arm.
Assign the effect to topology, kinetics, both, or neither by the pre-registered pattern.
Do not reinterpret the pattern after seeing it.
approaches.decisive_result: A four-way call: enrichment in A only (topology), B only (kinetics), both, or neither, using the same p-value and 20-of-35 rule in each arm.
approaches.failure_signature: Arm C differs from the first approach's null on the same seeds, which means the factor arms are not comparable. Substantively, enrichment in neither arm refutes a biological signature of either factor.

approaches.title: Prove habituation for one nonlinear motif and not for linear ODEs
approaches.method: Define habituation as three inequalities on a forced ODE: repeated identical pulses produce strictly decreasing peak responses; after a rest interval longer than a stated multiple of the pulse spacing, the next peak returns to within 10 percent of the first; the decrement happens for every pulse amplitude in an open interval. Prove that a three-variable system with slow negative feedback satisfies this on an open set of parameters. Prove that no linear system of the same input-output shape can satisfy decrement for all amplitudes in an interval and recovery after rest, because superposition fixes the gain. This shows habituation is generic for that motif and absent for linear kinetics. It does not show that BioModels are enriched. A failure here leaves the enrichment test untouched.
steps: Write the habituation inequalities as a Lean predicate.
Define the three-variable negative-feedback system.
Prove the predicate on an open parameter set.
Prove linear systems of the same shape fail the predicate.
Audit axioms.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry existence theorem for the nonlinear motif and a no-sorry impossibility theorem for linear kinetics, under the stated habituation predicate.
approaches.failure_signature: The nonlinear motif fails recovery or fails decrement on every open set tried, or a linear system is found that meets the predicate. Either kills the generic-versus-linear claim.

problems.title: A falsifiable form of active-inference morphogenesis
problems.question: Can the claim that morphogenesis is variational free-energy minimization be stated as a quantitative prediction that a regeneration or development experiment could refute, and does existing data refute it?
problems.known_state: Friston, Levin, Sengupta and Pezzulo (2015) modelled morphogenesis as active inference by identical cells sharing a generative model; Kuchling et al. (2020) extended it to regeneration. Critics hold the framework is unfalsifiable because any outcome can be described as free-energy minimization under some generative model. No prediction has been derived that fixes the generative model in advance and could fail. The repo's levin-2015-place and levin-2019-boundary claims are untested for this reason.
acceptance_criteria: A derivation, from a generative model fixed before looking at data, of a quantitative prediction (for example regeneration time or error rate scaling with a stated surprise measure under graded perturbations) together with the observation that would refute it.
A pre-registered test of that prediction on published planarian or Xenopus regeneration time courses.
falsifiers: If every candidate prediction can be rescued by changing the generative model post hoc, the framework is not empirically testable in its current form; that is itself a result.
problems.data_access: Published regeneration time courses (open-access Levin lab papers).

related_claims.label: Morphogenesis requires each cell to model its place in the target form
Free energy is minimized only when every cell occupies a unique inferred place
Cells in development minimize surprise and variational free energy like nervous systems
Regeneration as descent to a free-energy attractor; induced shapes as local minima

approaches.title: Lean: a finite complete-class theorem showing exactly when free-energy accounts are empty
approaches.method: Make the unfalsifiability charge precise, which is a result in itself. Setting: finite hidden-state space S, finite observations O, finite actions A, and a policy π: Oⁿ → A over a finite horizon. Theorem 1 (finite complete class): for every deterministic policy π there exist a generative model (prior over S, likelihood, and preference prior over outcomes) under which π minimizes expected free energy; the construction places preference mass on the outcomes π produces. So without constraints on the generative model, the claim 'morphogenesis minimizes free energy' excludes no behaviour. Theorem 2 (restoring content): if the likelihood and preference prior are fixed in advance (for example the target morphology and the cell-signalling likelihood from Friston et al. 2015's model), the set of free-energy-optimal policies is a proper subset, and there exist observable trajectories outside it, with an explicit separating example. This gives a formal criterion: an active-inference morphogenesis claim is testable iff it fixes the components named in Theorem 2.
steps: Define finite POMDP-style generative models and expected free energy over Finset types in Lean.
Prove Theorem 1 by explicit construction of the preference prior.
Prove Theorem 2 with a small explicit fixed model (for example 3 states, 2 actions) and a trajectory not optimal under it.
Write a short note mapping critics' and proponents' statements to Theorems 1 and 2.
approaches.decisive_result: Lean-checked Theorems 1 and 2. Together they state precisely that the framework is empty with a free generative model and testable with a fixed one, which turns the falsifiability debate into a checkable criterion that approaches 2 and 3 then meet.
approaches.failure_signature: Expected free energy has several non-equivalent definitions in the literature, and the theorems hold for one but not others; the result then must be stated per definition, which weakens its reach.

approaches.title: Fix Friston et al.'s generative model and derive a graded-excision prediction
approaches.method: Take the published generative model (Friston et al. 2015: cells with a shared model of target positions and signal expression) without modification and derive a quantitative prediction for an experiment that already exists. Simulate excision of fractions f ∈ {0.1, …, 0.9} of the ensemble and measure (a) time to reach the target configuration and (b) the probability of incorrect pattern (a residual error above threshold). The model predicts specific functional forms, for example recovery time increasing with f up to a critical fraction f_c beyond which the pattern fails. Freeze these predictions, functional forms and f_c with intervals over the model's stated parameter ranges, before collecting data. Then compare with published planarian regeneration data on fragment size versus regeneration success and time, and Xenopus or axolotl data where graded removals exist. Pre-registered: refuted if the observed success-versus-fragment-size curve is outside the predicted envelope at ≥ 2 fragment sizes.
steps: Reimplement the Friston et al. 2015 simulation from the published equations; reproduce its figures.
Run graded excisions over the model's parameter ranges; freeze predicted curves with envelopes.
Compile published fragment-size and regeneration-outcome data with a pre-registered inclusion rule.
Compare; report verdict and which model parameters, if any, the data constrain.
approaches.decisive_result: A pre-registered comparison of the fixed-model prediction (recovery time and failure probability versus fraction removed, with envelope) against published regeneration data. Observations outside the envelope refute this active-inference model of pattern regulation; observations inside it are a first non-trivial success.
approaches.failure_signature: The envelope over plausible parameters is so wide that it contains every monotone curve, so the fixed model still makes no risky prediction. This would confirm Theorem 1's warning in practice even with the model fixed.
approaches.missing: Published regeneration datasets reporting outcomes over graded fragment sizes are sparse and old; the decisive experiment would need new lab work.

approaches.title: Craniofacial remodelling: error-proportional correction vs hardwired movement
approaches.method: Xenopus 'Picasso' tadpoles, with organs experimentally displaced, remodel toward normal craniofacial geometry (Vandenberg et al. 2012; Pinet et al. 2019). A fixed-target active-inference model with Gaussian precision predicts that each organ's correction velocity is proportional to its displacement from the target, giving exponential relaxation and a rate independent of the direction of displacement. A hardwired-movement alternative (organs migrate a fixed program regardless of start) predicts velocity independent of displacement. Using organ positions reported or measurable in these papers' figures at multiple stages, estimate for each organ the regression of displacement change on initial displacement. Pre-registered: the active-inference model is supported if the slope is negative with exponential-fit R² ≥ 0.6, and refuted if velocity is independent of displacement (slope CI including 0) or if organs overshoot the target systematically, which a fixed-precision gradient flow cannot produce.
steps: Pre-register both models' predictions and the statistics.
Extract organ positions over developmental stages from the published figures and supplementary data, with landmark definitions.
Fit the displacement-dependent and displacement-independent models; compare by AICc.
Check for overshoot; report verdicts per organ.
approaches.decisive_result: Whether correction velocity scales with displacement (supporting fixed-target error correction) or not (supporting hardwired programs), per organ, with model-comparison weights. This is a risky prediction the fixed model can fail.
approaches.failure_signature: Published figures give too few time points or individuals per stage (fewer than 3 stages or 10 tadpoles), making slopes unidentifiable; or any proportional-correction result is shared by non-inferential gradient models, so it supports a class of models rather than active inference specifically (this must be stated in the interpretation).
approaches.missing: Individual-level trajectory data are not published as tables; figure extraction is limited and new time-lapse imaging would be decisive.

approaches.title: Frozen generative model predicts regeneration times
approaches.method: Choose one planarian regeneration series and fit a fixed generative model only to intact anatomy and unperturbed regeneration. Define sensory states, latent target morphology, likelihood variance and action dynamics before examining graded perturbations. Predict median regeneration time and failure probability as functions of initial variational surprise.
steps: Publish the full generative model, priors and fitting data split before testing.
Compute surprise from initial fragment geometry and Vmem summaries.
Derive posterior predictive time and error curves for held-out perturbations.
Compare against size-only and flexible survival-model baselines.
approaches.decisive_result: The fixed model passes if at least 80% of held-out median times lie within its 90% intervals and surprise improves leave-intervention-out ELPD by at least 10; failure of interval coverage below 50% refutes this instantiation.
approaches.failure_signature: Predictions require changing likelihoods, priors or target morphology after observing each perturbation, demonstrating post hoc flexibility.
approaches.missing: Open specimen-level regeneration time courses with quantified initial perturbations.

approaches.title: Identifiability and universal-fit stress test
approaches.method: Test falsifiability directly. Generate synthetic morphogenetic trajectories from reaction-diffusion, mechanical relaxation and random state-space models, then fit the same bounded active-inference model class without changing its latent dimension or priors. Estimate how often it fits non-active-inference processes as well as genuine ones.
steps: Predefine model class, parameter bounds and predictive scoring rule.
Generate 1000 datasets per mechanism over matched noise and sample sizes.
Fit blindly and perform simulation-based calibration.
Compute specificity, power and parameter identifiability for labeling active inference.
approaches.decisive_result: The framework is discriminative only if power and specificity both exceed 0.8 on held-out trajectories; specificity below 0.6 shows the tested formulation can absorb unrelated dynamics.
approaches.failure_signature: Equivalent predictive scores occur across all generators or posterior parameters are nonidentifiable, making empirical attribution unsupported.

approaches.title: Fix the generative model, then rank regeneration times
approaches.method: Before opening a regeneration time course, fix the generative model to the shared target morphology used by Friston, Levin, Sengupta and Pezzulo 2015, with no free retargeting. Define the surprise of a cut as the variational free energy of that initial condition under the fixed target. The prediction is ordinal: among fragment classes of one species in one paper, the ordering of free energies must match the ordering of regeneration times, with Spearman rank correlation above 0.5. Planarian fragment series are the admissible data, and only series that report times for at least four fragment classes. Parameters of the target are taken from the 2015 paper, not from the time series. Fewer than four classes, or times that exist only as unlabeled cartoons, makes the test inconclusive.
steps: Transcribe the 2015 target morphology and freeze it.
Define free energy of a cut under that target.
List fragment classes and published times from one admissible series.
Compute Spearman correlation between free-energy rank and time rank.
Refute the fixed model if the correlation is at most 0.5.
approaches.decisive_result: Spearman correlation above 0.5 between pre-registered free-energy rank and regeneration-time rank, on at least four fragment classes.
approaches.failure_signature: Correlation at most 0.5. Changing the target after seeing the times fails the approach and is the unfalsifiability pattern the problem names.
approaches.missing: Quantitative regeneration times for four or more fragment classes in one paper. If the papers only show cartoons, the test is inconclusive.

approaches.title: Prove the free-target class is tautological
approaches.method: Two theorems. First, if the generative model may be any smooth target morphology plus a positive precision, then for every observed morphology there exists a target equal to it that minimizes variational free energy. That class is unfalsifiable, and the theorem should say so. Second, with the target fixed as in the 2015 paper, the free-energy ordering of a finite set of cuts is not an identity: exhibit two cuts whose free-energy order is determined by the fixed target, so a reversed regeneration-time order would violate the prediction. The second theorem is the falsifiable form. If the fixed-target ordering can still be reversed by using a degree of freedom the paper leaves open, the second theorem fails and the approach concludes that the published model is not yet a test.
steps: Define variational free energy for a morphology and a target.
Prove existence of a minimizing target for every observation.
Instantiate the 2015 target and rank a finite set of cuts.
Show the ranking is invariant under the degrees of freedom the paper leaves free, or name the freedom that flips it.
Audit axioms.
approaches.decisive_result: A no-sorry tautology theorem for free targets, and either a no-sorry non-identity for the fixed 2015 target or a proof that a free parameter in that paper flips the ranking.
approaches.failure_signature: The fixed-target ranking flips under a parameter the pre-registration treated as frozen. The model is then not testable in the form stated, which the problem accepts as a result only if it is proved rather than asserted.

approaches.title: Lattice simulation with the target frozen before the cut
approaches.method: Implement the cell-lattice update from Kuchling et al. 2020 only if the paper states a complete parameter set. If it gives a schematic without numbers, stop and mark the approach not operationalizable. When numbers exist, freeze them, apply one cut geometry that the paper reports but that is not the figure used to illustrate the update, and predict the polarity class. frontier_simulate's mechanobiology preview may be used to check that a lattice energy is inside its allowlisted family; it does not replace the lattice run and is not evidence. Success is the published polarity class. One cut, named first.
steps: Extract numerical parameters from Kuchling et al. 2020 or stop.
Name the held-out cut before simulating.
Run the lattice update with the frozen target.
Compare predicted polarity with the paper.
Do not add a parameter to repair a miss.
approaches.decisive_result: The pre-named cut's published polarity, from a parameter set taken entirely from the paper.
approaches.failure_signature: The polarity is wrong, or the paper has no complete parameter set. The second case is a failed operationalization, not a refutation of active inference.
approaches.missing: A fully numerical parameter set in the paper. If the model is schematic, this approach cannot start.
